dolma.name: Dolma
dolma.summary: A family of stuffed dishes, mainly vegetables or leaves filled with rice, meat and spices, associated with Ottoman cuisine and spread across former Ottoman regions.

lower-mesopotamia.name: Lower Mesopotamia
lower-mesopotamia.summary: Southern alluvial plain of Iraq, home to the ancient civilizations of Sumer and Babylonia.

meze.name: meze
meze.summary: A selection of small appetizer dishes served in Eastern Mediterranean cuisines, similar to Spanish tapas, often accompanied by spirits such as ouzo or raki.

manakish.name: Manakish
manakish.summary: A popular Levantine pastry of dough topped with za'atar, cheese, or meat, traditionally baked by women in communal ovens and recognized by UNESCO in 2023 as part of Lebanon's culinary heritage.

kibbeh.name: Kibbeh
kibbeh.summary: A popular Levantine dish of spiced ground meat and bulgur wheat, considered a national dish of Lebanon and Syria, with many regional variations.

ful-medames.name: Ful medames
ful-medames.summary: A stew of cooked fava beans seasoned with olive oil and spices, considered Egypt's national dish and a staple food there since at least the 17th century.

baba-ghanoush.name: Baba ghanoush
baba-ghanoush.summary: A Levantine appetizer of roasted eggplant mixed with olive oil, lemon juice and tahini, traditionally smoked over an open flame and served as a meze.

masgouf.name: Masgouf
masgouf.summary: A Mesopotamian dish of seasoned, grilled carp, often considered the national dish of Iraq.

upper-mesopotamia.name: Upper Mesopotamia
upper-mesopotamia.summary: The uplands and plain of northwestern Iraq, northeastern Syria and southeastern Turkey, known since the 7th century as al-Jazira, 'the island,' between the Tigris and Euphrates.

hasakah-governorate.name: Hasakah Governorate
hasakah-governorate.summary: A governorate in the far northeast corner of Syria, formerly known as al-Jazira Province, noted for fertile lands, water, and over a hundred archaeological sites.

khabur.name: Khabur
khabur.summary: The largest perennial tributary of the Euphrates in Syria, originating in Turkey, whose valley has been a vital water source for agriculture throughout history.

mandatory-palestine.name: Mandatory Palestine
mandatory-palestine.summary: British-administered territory in Palestine from 1920 to 1948 under a League of Nations mandate, established after the Balfour Declaration and the fall of Ottoman rule.

freekeh.name: Freekeh
freekeh.summary: An ancient cereal food made from green durum wheat that is roasted, rubbed and dried, remaining popular across the eastern Mediterranean since wheat was first domesticated there.

robert-koldewey.name: Robert Koldewey
robert-koldewey.summary: German archaeologist (1855-1925) who led the excavation of ancient Babylon from 1899, uncovering the Ishtar Gate and developing techniques for excavating mudbrick architecture like the Hanging Gardens.

leonard-woolley.name: Leonard Woolley
leonard-woolley.summary: A British archaeologist (1880-1960) best known for his methodical excavations at Ur in Mesopotamia, recognized as one of the first modern archaeologists to excavate carefully and reconstruct ancient life and history; knighted in 1935 for his contributions to archaeology.

ur.name: Ur
ur.summary: A major Sumerian city-state in ancient Mesopotamia dating from about 3800 BC, whose patron deity was the moon god Nanna and whose ziggurat still stands partially restored.

royal-cemetery-at-ur.name: Royal Cemetery at Ur
royal-cemetery-at-ur.summary: An archaeological site in southern Iraq excavated between 1922 and 1934 by Leonard Woolley for the British Museum and University of Pennsylvania, its finds now held mainly in Baghdad and London.

ram-in-a-thicket.name: Ram in a Thicket
ram-in-a-thicket.summary: A pair of ancient figures excavated at Ur in southern Iraq, dating from about 2600–2400 BC, now held in the British Museum and the University of Pennsylvania Museum.

lyres-of-ur.name: Lyres of Ur
lyres-of-ur.summary: A set of four stringed instruments (three lyres and a harp) excavated at the Royal Cemetery of Ur from 1922 onward, dating to about 2550–2450 BC and the world's oldest surviving stringed instruments.

ishtar-gate.name: Ishtar Gate
ishtar-gate.summary: The eighth gate of Babylon's inner city wall, built around 569 BC under King Nebuchadnezzar II, decorated with glazed-brick animals and deities; excavated by Robert Koldewey from 1904 to 1914.

nuri-al-rawi.name: Nuri al-Rawi
nuri-al-rawi.summary: An Iraqi painter (1925–2014) and pioneer of Iraqi modern art who also worked as an author, television presenter, and art critic.

mohammed-ghani-hikmat.name: Mohammed Ghani Hikmat
mohammed-ghani-hikmat.summary: Iraqi sculptor (1929–2011) known as the "sheik of sculptors," a founder of early Iraqi modern art groups who later helped recover artworks looted after the 2003 invasion.

ziggurat-of-ur.name: Ziggurat of Ur
ziggurat-of-ur.summary: A Neo-Sumerian temple tower built in the 21st century BC by King Ur-Nammu at Ur, later restored, excavated in the 1920s–30s, and partly rebuilt under Saddam Hussein.

walter-andrae.name: Walter Andrae
walter-andrae.summary: A German archaeologist and architect (1875–1956) born near Leipzig.

vorderasiatisches-museum-berlin.name: Vorderasiatisches Museum Berlin
vorderasiatisches-museum-berlin.summary: An archaeological museum in Berlin's Pergamon Museum holding one of the world's largest collections of Southwest Asian art, spanning six millennia from Sumer, Babylonia, and Assyria.

jawad-saleem.name: Jawad Saleem
jawad-saleem.summary: An Iraqi painter and sculptor (1919–1961) considered one of Iraq's greatest 20th-century sculptors, a founder of the Baghdad Group for Modern Art, known for the Nasb al-Hurriyya monument.

shakir-hassan-al-said.name: Shakir Hassan Al Said
shakir-hassan-al-said.summary: An Iraqi painter, sculptor and writer (1925-2004) considered one of Iraq's most influential artists, who helped shape the country's modern art movement.

hashemites.name: Hashemites
hashemites.summary: The royal family of Jordan since 1921, and formerly of Hejaz, Syria, and Iraq, which ruled Mecca continuously from the 10th century and traces its ancestry to the Prophet Muhammad's family.

14-july-revolution.name: 1958 Revolution
14-july-revolution.summary: Military coup on 14 July 1958 that toppled King Faisal II and ended the Hashemite monarchy in Iraq, establishing the Iraqi Republic.

madiha-omar.name: Madiha Omar
madiha-omar.summary: Iraqi artist (1908-2005) regarded as the first Arab artist to combine calligraphy with abstract art, seen as a precursor to the Hurufiyya movement.

rafa-al-nasiri.name: Rafa al-Nasiri
rafa-al-nasiri.summary: Iraqi painter, draughtsman, print-maker, educator and author (1940–2013) whose socially and politically charged work resonated with the Iraqi public and inspired young print-makers.

sarin.name: Sarin
sarin.summary: An extremely toxic nerve agent and chemical weapon that can kill within minutes of exposure; its production has been banned worldwide since 1997.

fao-landing.name: Fao Landing
fao-landing.summary: A British military operation against Ottoman forces at Fao in November 1914, the first action of the Mesopotamian Campaign in World War I, undertaken to protect British oil supplies.

anglo-persian-oil-company.name: Anglo-Persian Oil Company
anglo-persian-oil-company.summary: A British company founded in 1909 after a major oil discovery in Persia; the British government took a controlling 51% stake in 1914, and it later became British Petroleum.

khuzestan-province.name: Khuzestan province
khuzestan-province.summary: A province in southwestern Iran bordering Iraq and the Persian Gulf, corresponding to ancient Elam whose capital was Susa; it holds Iran's largest oil field.

shatt-al-arab.name: Shatt al-Arab
shatt-al-arab.summary: A roughly 200-kilometre river formed where the Euphrates and Tigris meet in southern Iraq, flowing into the Persian Gulf and forming part of the Iran–Iraq border.

mesopotamian-campaign.name: Mesopotamian campaign
mesopotamian-campaign.summary: A World War I front in Ottoman Iraq, fought from 1914 to 1918 between the British Empire and the Ottoman Empire, including a major British defeat at Kut and the capture of Baghdad in 1917.

iraqi-republican-guard.name: Iraqi Republican Guard
iraqi-republican-guard.summary: An elite branch of the Iraqi military active from 1969 to 2003, mainly under President Saddam Hussein, better trained and equipped than the regular army, and disbanded after the 2003 invasion.

kut.name: Kut
kut.summary: A city in eastern Iraq on the Tigris River southeast of Baghdad, long a regional center of the carpet trade in a fertile grain-growing area.

siege-of-kut.name: Siege of Kut
siege-of-kut.summary: A 1915–1916 siege in which the Ottoman Army trapped and forced the surrender of a British Indian garrison in Kut, Iraq, called the worst Allied defeat of World War I.

winston-churchill.name: Winston Churchill
winston-churchill.summary: British statesman and Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and 1951 to 1955, who led Britain through the Second World War.

ethyl-iodoacetate.name: Ethyl iodoacetate
ethyl-iodoacetate.summary: An organic compound, a clear light yellow to orange liquid, historically used as a tear gas.

popular-front-for-the-liberation-of-pale.name: PFLP
popular-front-for-the-liberation-of-pale.summary: A Palestinian Marxist–Leninist organization founded in 1967 by George Habash, the second-largest group within the PLO after Fatah, known for pioneering aircraft hijackings.
popular-front-for-the-liberation-of-pale.source_title: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine

trans-arabian-pipeline.name: Trans-Arabian Pipeline
trans-arabian-pipeline.summary: An oil pipeline from Qaisumah in Saudi Arabia to Sidon in Lebanon, active from 1950 to 1976; it shaped global oil trade and American-Middle Eastern relations and aided Lebanon's economy.

saudi-aramco.name: Saudi Aramco
saudi-aramco.summary: Saudi Arabia's majority state-owned national oil and gas company, headquartered in Dhahran, holding the world's largest proven crude oil reserves and largest daily oil production of any oil company.

armistice-of-mudros.name: Armistice of Mudros
armistice-of-mudros.summary: Agreement signed on 30 October 1918 ending hostilities between the Ottoman Empire and the Allies in the Middle Eastern theatre of World War I, leading to Allied occupation and the partition of Ottoman territory.

alexander-cobbe.name: Alexander Cobbe
alexander-cobbe.summary: A senior British Indian Army officer (1870-1931) and recipient of the Victoria Cross, Britain's highest award for gallantry in the face of the enemy.

mosul.name: Mosul
mosul.summary: Major city in northern Iraq on the Tigris, near the ruins of ancient Nineveh, and a long-standing hub of regional trade and diverse peoples.

mosul-vilayet.name: Mosul Vilayet
mosul-vilayet.summary: Ottoman province created in 1878 around the city of Mosul, whose oil-rich territory became a major international dispute after the First World War.

challenger-1.name: Challenger 1
challenger-1.summary: A British main battle tank used by the British Army from 1983 to 2001, later sold largely to Jordan, where it remained in service until 2023.

t-54-t-55.name: T-54/T-55
t-54-t-55.summary: A series of Soviet medium tanks introduced after World War II, the most-produced tank design in history, with an estimated 96,500 to 100,000 built.

high-explosive-squash-head.name: HESH
high-explosive-squash-head.summary: An explosive shell that flattens plastic explosive against a target before detonating; not armour-piercing, but it can disable armoured vehicles by causing spall inside them.

najaf.name: Najaf
najaf.summary: A city in central Iraq holding the Imam Ali Shrine, burial place of Muhammad's son-in-law Ali, considered Shia Islam's holiest site after Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem.

william-marshall-british-army-officer-bo.name: William Marshall
william-marshall-british-army-officer-bo.summary: British Army officer (1865–1939) who became commander-in-chief of British forces in Mesopotamia in November 1917, holding the post through the end of World War I.

dunsterforce.name: Dunsterforce
dunsterforce.summary: Small Allied military force established in December 1917 and named for its commander, sent to organise local resistance in northern Iran and the South Caucasus.

lionel-dunsterville.name: Lionel Dunsterville
lionel-dunsterville.summary: British Indian Army major-general (1865–1946) who led Dunsterforce across Iraq and Iran toward the Caucasus and Baku during the First World War.

sinai-and-palestine-campaign.name: Sinai and Palestine campaign
sinai-and-palestine-campaign.summary: A World War I campaign (1915–1918) in which the British Empire and allies fought the Ottoman Empire, ending with the Ottomans' loss of Syria.

psalm-137.name: Psalm 137
psalm-137.summary: A psalm from the Book of Psalms beginning 'By the rivers of Babylon,' lamenting exile and longing for Jerusalem during the Babylonian captivity; still used in Jewish and Christian liturgy today.

leonard-cohen.name: Leonard Cohen
leonard-cohen.summary: A Canadian singer-songwriter, poet and novelist (1934–2016) whose work explored faith, mortality, love and loss; inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and made a Companion of the Order of Canada.

babylonian-captivity.name: Babylonian captivity
babylonian-captivity.summary: The exile of Judeans from the Kingdom of Judah to Babylonia by the Neo-Babylonian Empire after sieges of Jerusalem in 597 and 587 BCE, ending when Persia allowed their return in 539 BCE.

arthur-c-clarke.name: Arthur C. Clarke
arthur-c-clarke.summary: An English science fiction writer and futurist (1917–2008) known for popularising space travel and co-writing the screenplay for 2001: A Space Odyssey.

epic-of-gilgamesh.name: Epic of Gilgamesh
epic-of-gilgamesh.summary: The world's oldest surviving work of narrative literature, from ancient Mesopotamia, telling of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and his companion Enkidu; its standard version dates to the 13th–10th centuries BCE.

elizabeth-goudge.name: Elizabeth Goudge
elizabeth-goudge.summary: English writer of fiction and children's books who won the 1946 Carnegie Medal for The Little White Horse, later cited by J. K. Rowling as an influence.

herod-the-great.name: Herod the Great
herod-the-great.summary: Roman client king of Judea (c. 72–4/1 BCE) noted for vast building projects including rebuilding the Second Temple; the Christian Bible names him as ordering the Massacre of the Innocents.

electronic-text-corpus-of-sumerian-liter.name: ETCSL
electronic-text-corpus-of-sumerian-liter.summary: An online digital library of Sumerian texts and English translations, covering over 400 literary works from ancient Mesopotamia, founded in 1997 at Oxford.
electronic-text-corpus-of-sumerian-liter.source_title: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature

nazik-al-malaika.name: Nazik Al-Malaika
nazik-al-malaika.summary: An Iraqi poet, 1923 to 2007, noted as among the first Arabic poets to write free verse.

al-wathbah-uprising.name: Al-Wathbah uprising
al-wathbah-uprising.summary: Urban unrest in Baghdad in January 1948, sparked by plans to renew the 1930 Anglo-Iraqi Treaty, which forced the government to drop the renewal.

urukagina.name: Urukagina
urukagina.summary: King of the Mesopotamian city-states of Lagash and Girsu in the 24th century BC (died c. 2368 BC), the last ruler of Lagash's 1st Dynasty, whose reign ended when Lagash was destroyed in war against rival Umma.

samuel-noah-kramer.name: Samuel Noah Kramer
samuel-noah-kramer.summary: An Assyriologist (1897–1990) and leading expert on Sumerian history and language, whose book History Begins at Sumer made the subject accessible to the public.

cuneiform-digital-library-initiative.name: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative
cuneiform-digital-library-initiative.summary: An international project, begun in 1998, to put images and text of an estimated 500,000 ancient cuneiform tablets online for research.

pennsylvania-sumerian-dictionary.name: Pennsylvania Sumerian Dictionary
pennsylvania-sumerian-dictionary.summary: A project, begun in 1974 at the University of Pennsylvania, to compile a comprehensive dictionary of the Sumerian language, later reworked into an online edition.

iraq-petroleum-company.name: Iraq Petroleum Company
iraq-petroleum-company.summary: An oil company, formerly called the Turkish Petroleum Company, that held a virtual monopoly on oil exploration and production in Iraq from 1925 until it was nationalized in 1961/1972.

kirkuk.name: Kirkuk
kirkuk.summary: A major city in northern Iraq and capital of Kirkuk Governorate, home to a mixed population of Kurds, Iraqi Turkmens and Arabs, whose contested status remains unresolved despite a 2005 constitutional process meant to settle it.

baba-gurgur.name: Baba Gurgur
baba-gurgur.summary: An oil field and gas flame near Kirkuk, Iraq, discovered in 1927 and considered the world's largest oil field until Saudi Arabia's Ghawar field was found in 1948.

qaisumah.name: Qaisumah
qaisumah.summary: A small town in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, the starting point of the Trans-Arabian Pipeline built beginning in 1947.

sidon.name: Sidon
sidon.summary: Third-largest city in Lebanon, on the Mediterranean coast, capital of the South Governorate, located between Tyre and Beirut.

bechtel.name: Bechtel
bechtel.summary: An American engineering and construction company founded in San Francisco in 1898, one of the largest construction firms in the United States.

kirkuk-field.name: Kirkuk Field
kirkuk-field.summary: An oilfield in Kirkuk, Iraq, discovered in 1927 and brought into production in 1934, long one of the most important sources of northern Iraqi oil with over 10 billion barrels of proven reserves recorded in 1998.

nineveh.name: Nineveh
nineveh.summary: Ancient city on the Tigris near modern Mosul, Iraq, and capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire; briefly the largest city in the world until it was sacked in 612 BC.

british-raj.name: British Raj
british-raj.summary: Period of direct rule by the British Crown over the Indian subcontinent, from 1858 until 1947, when it was partitioned into India and Pakistan.

mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.name: French Mandate for Syria and Lebanon
mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.summary: A League of Nations mandate (1923–1946) that gave France administrative control over Syria and Lebanon after the Ottoman Empire's partition following World War I.
mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon.source_title: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon

sayfo.name: Sayfo
sayfo.summary: The mass killing and deportation of Assyrian/Syriac Christians in southeastern Anatolia and Persia's Azerbaijan province by Ottoman forces and Kurdish tribes during World War I.

simele-massacre.name: Simele massacre
simele-massacre.summary: A 1933 massacre of Assyrians by the Kingdom of Iraq around the village of Simele, which shaped modern Assyrian identity and influenced the coining of the term genocide.

faisal-i.name: Faisal I
faisal-i.summary: Hashemite leader of the Great Arab Revolt who briefly ruled as king of the unrecognized Arab Kingdom of Syria in 1920 before French expulsion, then became king of Iraq from 1921 to 1933.

deir-ez-zor.name: Deir ez-Zor
deir-ez-zor.summary: The largest city in eastern Syria, on the Euphrates 280 miles northeast of Damascus, and capital of its governorate.

panbabylonism.name: Panbabylonism
panbabylonism.summary: An early 20th-century school of thought, mainly among German Assyriologists, holding that Middle Eastern cultures and religions derived from Babylonian astronomy and myth.

hugo-winckler.name: Hugo Winckler
hugo-winckler.summary: German orientalist, archaeologist and historian (1863–1913) who uncovered the Hittite capital of Hattusa and translated the Code of Hammurabi.

liturgy-of-addai-and-mari.name: Liturgy of Addai and Mari
liturgy-of-addai-and-mari.summary: A Eucharistic liturgy of the East Syriac Rite historically used in the Church of the East of the Sasanian Empire, traditionally attributed to disciples Saint Addai and Saint Mari.

words-of-institution.name: Words of Institution
words-of-institution.summary: Words echoing those Jesus spoke at the Last Supper, included by almost all ancient Christian churches when consecrating the bread and wine of the Eucharist.

dicastery-for-the-doctrine-of-the-faith.name: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith
dicastery-for-the-doctrine-of-the-faith.summary: Department of the Roman Curia responsible for defending Catholic doctrine, founded in 1542 as the Roman Inquisition and renamed several times before becoming the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith in 1965.
dicastery-for-the-doctrine-of-the-faith.source_title: Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith

susa.name: Susa
susa.summary: Ancient city in what is now Iran that served as capital of Elam and winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire, remaining strategically important through the Parthian and Sasanian periods.

alexander-hislop.name: Alexander Hislop
alexander-hislop.summary: A Free Church of Scotland minister (1807-1865) and critic of the Catholic Church, best known for his book The Two Babylons, arguing Catholic practices descended from ancient Babylon.

the-two-babylons.name: The Two Babylons
the-two-babylons.summary: An 1853 book by Presbyterian theologian Alexander Hislop (1807–1865) arguing that the Catholic Church is the Babylon of Revelation and that its holidays descend from pagan festivals; modern scholars reject its arguments.

arthur-pink.name: A. W. Pink
arthur-pink.summary: An English Bible teacher (1886–1952) who sparked renewed interest in Calvinism and became a widely influential evangelical author.

the-watchtower.name: The Watchtower
the-watchtower.summary: An illustrated religious magazine published by Jehovah's Witnesses' Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, distributed with its companion Awake! and reporting circulation of over 31 million copies in 461 languages.

ugarit.name: Ugarit
ugarit.summary: An ancient Levantine coastal city in what is now northern Syria, also known as Ras Shamra; excavations since 1928 revealed the oldest known systematic use of an alphabet.

zoroastrianism.name: Zoroastrianism
zoroastrianism.summary: An ancient Iranian religion founded on the teachings of Zoroaster, centred on the deity Ahura Mazda and the choice between truth and chaos, once Greater Iran's dominant faith under the Sassanid Empire.

government-of-the-kurdistan-region.name: Kurdistan Regional Government
government-of-the-kurdistan-region.summary: The official executive body of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region, headed by a president who also commands the Peshmerga forces.

kemalism.name: Kemalism
kemalism.summary: The political ideology of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of Turkey, marked by secularizing and modernizing reforms that separated the new republic from its Ottoman predecessor.

uruk-period.name: Uruk period
uruk-period.summary: The era, roughly 4000 to 3100 BC, when the first cities and states arose in Mesopotamia, named after the city of Uruk where innovations like the potter's wheel appeared.

uruk.name: Uruk
uruk.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian city that, at its peak around 3100 BC, may have been the largest urban settlement in the world, with tens of thousands of residents.

bah-faith.name: Baháʼí Faith
bah-faith.summary: A religion founded by Baháʼu'lláh in 19th-century Iran teaching the unity of all religions and people, with 7 to 8 million followers worldwide today.

dinkha-iv.name: Dinkha IV
dinkha-iv.summary: Eastern Christian prelate (1935–2015) who served as Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East, the first patriarch not from the Shimun family since 1672.

raphael-i-bidawid.name: Raphael I Bidawid
raphael-i-bidawid.summary: Patriarch of the Chaldean Catholic Church from 1989 to 2003 and a Syriac scholar.

chaldean-catholic-church.name: Chaldean Catholic Church
chaldean-catholic-church.summary: An Eastern Catholic church descended from the Church of the East, formed through a 1552 schism and led today by the Patriarch of Baghdad, with about 617,000 members worldwide.

girsu.name: Girsu
girsu.summary: An ancient Sumerian city about 25 km northwest of Lagash, in what is now Iraq, that served as Lagash's religious center with major temples to the god Ningirsu.

ningirsu.name: Ningirsu
ningirsu.summary: Mesopotamian god who was tutelary deity of the city of Girsu and chief god of Lagash's pantheon, with warlike and agricultural-fertility aspects.

nanshe.name: Nanshe
nanshe.summary: A Mesopotamian goddess linked to the sea, marshlands, birds and fish, as well as divination, justice and social welfare, worshipped across Mesopotamia for centuries.

yasna.name: Yasna
yasna.summary: Both a text within the Avesta and the principal act of worship in Zoroastrianism.

mesopotamia_levant-modern-literature-005: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature
